conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you came in with worsening upper abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me what today has been like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same burning pain in the middle, but way worse this morning. Even water makes it flare. I threw up once—just watery, not bloody.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, chest pain, trouble breathing, or black or bloody stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I had a bowel movement this morning and I’m passing gas. I just feel a little bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Given your history—Roux-en-Y bypass with reversal, ulcers, tube feeds—we’re taking this seriously. In the ED your bloodwork looked reassuring: no infection signs, electrolytes okay, liver tests and lipase normal, and lactate normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much if the labs are normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can still be severe even when labs are normal, especially with chronic ulcer-type pain, reflux, and changes after multiple abdominal surgeries. We also want to rule out dangerous things like obstruction or a perforation—those can sometimes show up on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you thinking I need surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bariatric surgery already evaluated you in the ED and they don’t think you need surgical intervention right now. Our plan is medical management: pain and nausea control, acid suppression, and careful diet advancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat? Last time they told me not to take anything by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For tonight we’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—so we can settle things down and make sure there’s no obstruction. We’ll continue your tube feeds at your goal rate so you’re still getting nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared the tube feeds will make the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Since you’ve been on continuous feeds at home, we expect you can tolerate them, but if it clearly worsens symptoms we’ll reassess. We’ll also treat nausea so you’re more comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you giving me for pain? Tylenol doesn’t touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use a stepwise approach: acetaminophen as needed, and your liquid oxycodone as needed for breakthrough pain. We’ll also continue your pantoprazole and sucralfate to protect the stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin, so I can’t take those anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—so we’ll avoid them. We’ll also use ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back—no free air under the diaphragm and no acute lung issues. That’s reassuring against a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the belly X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows a nonobstructive bowel gas pattern—no signs of a small bowel obstruction, and no free air. Your G-tube is seen in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not blocked. Then why does drinking water hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With reflux or ulcer irritation, even small amounts of liquid can trigger burning pain. Also, after multiple surgeries, the stomach and intestines can have altered motility—things don’t move as smoothly, which can cause discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this just going to keep happening? I’ve been in the hospital so many times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Part of our work this admission is symptom control, but also setting a realistic plan: this may not fully resolve in a day or two. We want to stabilize you and coordinate with your bariatric and GI teams to build a regimen that improves quality of life over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any more vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more vomiting. Still nauseated on and off. Pain is a little better after meds but it’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your morning labs are stable—no electrolyte problems and no signs of infection. We’d like to try advancing you to clear liquids by mouth today, very slowly, while continuing tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What counts as clear liquids? And what if it burns again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sips of water, clear nutritional drinks if tolerated. If it flares, stop and let us know—this is a trial, not a test you have to push through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a few sips. It stung but I didn’t throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful information. We’ll keep it slow. We’re also thinking about bacterial overgrowth and dysmotility contributing to symptoms, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my ammonia was high before? They told me it might be overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, bacterial overgrowth can contribute to symptoms like bloating, discomfort, and sometimes lab abnormalities. It’s not the only possibility, but it’s one piece we can treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you going to do for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start a short trial of erythromycin. In low doses it can help gut motility, and sometimes that reduces nausea and pain related to slow movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that an antibiotic? I’m worried about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is an antibiotic, but here we’re using it mainly for its motility effect. We’ll use a limited course and watch for stomach upset. If it makes things worse, we’ll stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: how are the clear liquids going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do small sips. I’m still scared to eat. I don’t want to trigger it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. Our goal isn’t to force solid food right now. We’ll keep tube feeds as your main nutrition and use oral intake as gentle practice—water and maybe an Ensure-type shake if tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My reflux feels worse when I lie down. Is there anything else besides pantoprazole and sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We can add ranitidine at night to help with nighttime acid and reflux symptoms. It works differently than pantoprazole, so the combination can help some people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that interfere with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s generally compatible with your current regimen. We’ll keep an eye on how you feel, and you should continue taking sucralfate as prescribed since it coats the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today compared with when you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not gone, but it’s steadier. I haven’t thrown up again. I did okay with cream of wheat and a little pudding yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your exam is reassuring—your abdomen is soft and only minimally tender, and the G-tube site looks okay without redness or warmth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you know if I have H. pylori again? I’ve had ulcers before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent H. pylori blood testing. The result isn’t back yet, so it will be pending at discharge. We’ll make sure the outpatient team follows it, and we’ll also tell you how to check the result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it’s positive, what happens?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s positive, your doctors would prescribe a specific combination of medications to eradicate it. For now, we’re continuing strong acid suppression and lining protection, which is appropriate either way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge later today if you continue to tolerate tube feeds and small amounts by mouth and your pain stays controlled with your home regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home. What if it spikes again tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The key is having a clear plan: continue tube feeds at your goal rate, keep oral intake gentle, and use your prescribed nausea and pain meds. If you can’t keep anything down, have repeated vomiting, severe worsening pain, black or bloody stools, fever, or you feel faint—those are reasons to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you changing my tube feed formula? I use Jevity 1.2 at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition recommends Jevity 1.5 at 50 mL/hour as a goal. If you’re staying on 1.2 for now, your outpatient provider who manages tube feeds can adjust and write the prescription if a change is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What new meds am I leaving with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two main additions: ranitidine 150 mg nightly for reflux, and a short course of erythromycin 250 mg three times daily. We’re also adding rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for a short course to target possible bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rifaximin is expensive, isn’t it? I can’t afford another medication I can’t fill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with your home pharmacy and it should be affordable. If there’s any issue at pickup, call the bariatric clinic right away so they can help troubleshoot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I take the erythromycin and rifaximin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re short courses—about a week. At your bariatric surgery follow-up, you’ll review whether they’re helping and decide whether to continue or stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the goal is not that I’m pain-free, just stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want you safe—no obstruction, no dehydration, no ongoing vomiting—and on a plan that gradually improves symptoms. With your surgical history, it often takes weeks to months of careful adjustments with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review: continue pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate four times daily, add ranitidine nightly, finish erythromycin and rifaximin as prescribed, keep tube feeds running, and slowly advance oral intake as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I can only do water and shakes for a while, that’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Water and Ensure-type shakes are a reasonable start. Add solids very slowly over weeks to months, only as tolerated, and keep close follow-up with bariatric surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want my life back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal, and we’ll keep working toward it with you. You’re leaving in stable condition, and you can always reach out if symptoms change or you’re worried.
